coverage: Round 3, academic angle. Roster: the 54-entry Fedwren Project bibliography (read in full) plus four works chased from Oliver's works-cited and eighteen further items surfaced by an OpenAlex "Robin Hobb" sweep (115 records, three pages read). Fetched and read at the primary: Oliver (Mythlore 2022, the crown source, read entire), Ekman and Taylor (JFA 2021, via Wayback), Lagus (Helsinki 2006), Moon (Kent 2024), Duits and Kok (Utrecht 2012, via the DSpace REST API), Freeman (UTS 2006), Elliott's three papers (Words like Coins 2013, Sites of Memory 2021, Another Update 2026) and his bibliography, Tkach and Volkova (onomastics 2026), Srsic (Studia Anglica Resoviensia 2025), Garnes (Estudios de Traduccion 2016), Waumans (PLoS ONE 2015), Dekker (PeerJ CS 2019, via Wayback), Slavova (2019 and 2020). Abstract-only: Borowska-Szerszun 2019, Melville 2018, Young 2014 (all closed at Liverpool UP; OpenAlex records). Relay only: Mandala 2010 (no open copy anywhere, reached through Wikipedia's Farseer Style section), Mendlesohn 2008 (archive.org lending-restricted, reached through Oliver's verbatim quotation), Shropshire 2019, Crane and Fletcher 2017 and Bruening 2014 (reached through Elliott's annotations). Blocked or not found: Bokne 2018 (gupea Anubis 500), Shropshire 2019 (absent from SHAREOK's index), Google Books (API day quota exhausted by earlier lanes), diva-portal and peerj and academia.edu (refused; Wayback used instead). Not fetched by judgement: the roster's fandom/copyright cluster (Busse, Flegel and Roth, Roth and Flegel, Stein and Busse, Hautsch, Young in Reason, Wilkins) and the gender-studies theses (Katavic, Metsapelto, Mohon, Nordlund, Rasanen, Sanderson, Schouwenaars), none of which treat prose style, register or place description. 21 substantive sources read of 31 fetched; 73 claims. Stop rule met: the last two lateral searches returned only sources already read.

claims.claim: Every chapter of Assassin's Apprentice opens with a long epigraph excerpted from an in-world history of the Six Duchies.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver (Campbellsville University), 'History in the Margins: Epigraphs and Negative Space in Robin Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice', Mythlore 41.1 (Fall/Winter 2022) 45-66
claims.quote: Each chapter of the novel begins with a lengthy epigraph
claims.routeHint: SWOSU Digital Commons PDF (dc.swosu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi article=1447 context=mythlore); the landing page 403s to a plain fetch, the PDF does not

claims.claim: Oliver characterises the register of those in-world history epigraphs as a formal history in a distant, scholarly voice, set against the personal first-person narrative that follows.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: largely a formal history written in a distant, scholarly voice

claims.claim: Oliver calls the chapter-opening history dry and impersonal, and says the personal main text feels more authoritative and satisfying than it does.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: the dry, impersonal, but objective history beginning the chapter

claims.claim: The chapter-13 epigraph describing Fitz's stepmother Patience carries no sign of the writer's own relationship to her.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: contains no hint of the author's relationship to her

claims.claim: In place of personal knowledge the Patience epigraph cites testimony from her nursemaids and publicly available information.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: evidentiary quotes from her nursemaids and publicly available information

claims.claim: Oliver names the novel's most striking stylistic element its continual insistence on describing what is not happening.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: continual insistence on describing what is not happening

claims.claim: The device Oliver labels 'negative narration' works through sentences that open by saying what a character is not doing or feeling.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: sentences that start by telling what a character is not doing

claims.claim: Negative constructions are so frequent in the novel's early chapters that scarcely a page passes without obvious examples.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: scarcely a page goes by without obvious examples

claims.claim: Although the frequency of negative constructions falls off later, Oliver says the mode remains one of the book's predominant ones throughout.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: remains one of the predominant modes throughout

claims.claim: When Fitz invents a prophetic vision to persuade a duchess, his sentences shift into extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language and parallelism.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: extensive parataxis, elevated figurative language, and parallelism

claims.claim: Oliver reads that stylistic shift as marking Fitz's move from a discourse of history into a discourse of fantasy.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: Fitz marks his shift from a discourse of history

claims.claim: Late in the novel the epigraphs take on the style of imaginative fiction in place of the style of scholarly discourse.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: increasingly infected by the style of imaginative fiction

claims.claim: At the chapter-15 epigraph a poetic lyricism enters the register of the supposedly scholarly history.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: a poetic lyricism creeps into his style in the epigraph

claims.claim: Oliver measures the epigraph's drift by counting its inverted-syntax sentences: two of them, alongside parataxis across sentence boundaries and listed parallel phrases.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: Two sentences use inverted syntax

claims.claim: A roughly seventy-page stretch of the novel is defined by the absence of a key fact that is never stated outright.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: marked by the absence of a key detail

claims.claim: At the moment Fitz's magic returns, the narration reports only what the two men are not doing and leaves what they are doing implied.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: we are told what they are not doing

claims.claim: Oliver argues that the withheld section trains the reader to see what is not there and to supply the connections.
claims.source: Matthew Oliver, Mythlore 41.1 (2022) 45-66
claims.quote: training the reader to see what is not there

claims.claim: Kok describes the Six Duchies nobility as having a custom of naming children after virtues or traits in hope the child will emulate the name.

claims.claim: Kok points out that Hobb's noble names are not fantastical-sounding but ordinary English words.
